column3: Chemicals in sunscreen are worse for you than a sunburn.
column9: Fear-based; Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: aad-sunscreen-safety; run 2: aad-sunscreen-safety; run 3: aad-sunscreen-safety
column15: The claim says the chemicals in sunscreen do more harm to your body than a sunburn does.
column16: Dermatology guidance points the other way. Sunburn is skin damage from UV exposure and raises long-term skin cancer risk, while regulators have not concluded that any sunscreen ingredients sold in the U.S. are unsafe. Some people do find certain sunscreens irritating, and that is a reason to try a different type, not to skip protection.

column3: You don't need sunscreen on cloudy days.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: aad-cloudy-days; run 2: aad-cloudy-days; run 3: aad-cloudy-days
column15: Sunscreen is not necessary on cloudy days.
column16: Clouds block some light but not most UV. Dermatology guidance says up to 80% of UV rays can still reach your skin on cloudy days, so skin can still be exposed to sun damage when the sky looks gray.

column3: Darker skin tones don't need sunscreen.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: aad-cloudy-days; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: People with darker skin tones do not need to wear sunscreen.
column16: Skin of every tone can be damaged by UV rays, and skin cancer can happen at any skin tone. Darker skin has more natural pigment, which gives some protection against sunburn, but it does not give full protection. Dermatology guidance says UV reaches the skin even on cloudy days, so the idea that anyone is exempt does not hold up.

column3: Put toothpaste on a pimple overnight to dry it out.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Applying toothpaste to a pimple overnight will dry it out and make it go away.
column16: Dermatology guidance does not recommend toothpaste for acne. Toothpaste is made for teeth, not skin, and some ingredients in it can irritate the skin, causing redness, peeling or dryness around the spot. Irritated skin can look worse and may take longer to settle.

column3: Rub lemon juice on dark spots to fade them.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Rubbing lemon juice on dark spots will fade them.
column16: Dermatology guidance does not recommend lemon juice for dark spots. It is acidic and can irritate skin, and citrus on skin that then meets sunlight can cause a burn-like reaction and leave darker marks. Dark spots usually fade with approaches that are better studied and gentler on skin.

column3: If you use a retinoid, wear sunscreen every day.
column13: run 1: aad-cloudy-days + aad-sunscreen-safety; run 2: aad-cloudy-days; run 3: aad-cloudy-days + aad-sunscreen-safety
column15: If you use a retinoid, you should wear sunscreen every day.
column16: Dermatology guidance commonly advises daily sunscreen for people who use retinoids, because retinoids can make skin more sensitive to sun and more prone to irritation. UV rays also reach your skin on cloudy days, so daily use makes sense even when the sky looks gray. Sunscreen has not been shown to be unsafe for regular use.

column3: Beef tallow is the best moisturizer for every skin type.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Beef tallow is the single best moisturizer for all skin types.
column16: Dermatology guidance does not name any one moisturizer as best for everyone, because skin types and needs differ. Animal fats can feel rich, but some people find heavy fats clog pores or irritate skin, especially if they are prone to breakouts. There is little good research showing tallow beats other moisturizers.

column3: Detox teas flush toxins out of your liver.
column9: Miracle claim; Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Drinking detox teas removes toxins from your liver.
column16: Your liver and kidneys already filter and clear waste on their own, and no good evidence shows a tea can speed this up or 'flush' the liver. Some teas have a laxative or diuretic effect, which can make you feel lighter but only reflects lost fluid, not removed toxins.

column3: Most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep each night.
column16: Major sleep and public health guidance recommends that adults get 7 or more hours of sleep per night for good health. Needs vary a little from person to person, but 7 hours is the commonly cited minimum for most adults. Regularly getting less is linked with higher risks for several health problems.

column3: If you don't hit 10,000 steps, walking doesn't count.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Walking only counts as exercise if you reach 10,000 steps in a day.
column16: Public health guidance counts walking as physical activity at any level, and research links health benefits to well below 10,000 steps a day. The 10,000 figure is a popular round number, not a threshold where benefits suddenly begin. More movement is generally better, but fewer steps still help.

column3: Strength training twice a week is good for long-term health.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Doing strength training two times per week supports your long-term health.
column16: Public health and medical guidelines for adults recommend muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week. It is linked with better muscle and bone strength, better metabolic health and lower risk of early death. The claim is modest and does not promise a cure or a specific result.

column3: Cold plunges cure anxiety.
column9: Miracle claim; Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Cold plunges, meaning immersion in very cold water, cure anxiety.
column16: Some small studies suggest cold water may lift mood for a short time, but there is no good evidence that it cures an anxiety disorder. Anxiety is usually managed with approaches like therapy, lifestyle changes and sometimes medication, and a cure is not something cold exposure can promise. Cold immersion can also be risky for some people, especially those with heart or blood pressure problems.

column3: Taping your mouth shut at night fixes sleep for everyone.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all; Miracle claim
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Taping your mouth shut at night improves sleep for every person.
column16: Sleep medicine guidance does not back mouth taping as a general fix for sleep, and the small amount of research on it is limited. Poor sleep has many causes, so no single step works for everyone. Covering the mouth can also make breathing harder for people with a blocked nose or a sleep breathing problem.

column3: This coin is guaranteed to 10x by next month. Get in before it's too late.
column9: Guaranteed results; Urgency; Unrealistic income; Absolute language
column13: run 1: sec-crypto-guaranteed-returns; run 2: sec-crypto-guaranteed-returns; run 3: sec-crypto-guaranteed-returns
column15: A crypto coin is said to be guaranteed to increase tenfold within a month, and you should buy in quickly.
column16: No legitimate investment can guarantee a return, and a promise of a tenfold gain in a month is a classic warning sign of fraud. Prices of speculative assets can fall as easily as they rise, so a sure outcome is not something anyone can know. The pressure to act before it is too late is meant to rush your decision.

column3: Checking your own credit score lowers it.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Looking at your own credit score or credit report lowers your score.
column16: Checking your own score or report is treated as a soft inquiry, which does not affect your score. Lenders only run hard inquiries when you apply for credit, and a few of those can cause a small, temporary dip. Mixing up the two types is where this belief tends to start.

column3: Buy now, pay later is basically free money.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: The claim says buy now, pay later plans are essentially free money because you get items now and pay for them later.
column16: Some plans charge no interest if every payment is made on time, so they can work like a short, free loan for some people. Late fees, missed payments, and overspending can turn a plan into a real cost, and several plans at once can be hard to track. Calling it free money leaves out that it is still debt you owe.

column3: Pay off high-interest credit card debt before investing extra money.
column13: run 1: sec-pay-high-interest-debt + fed-g19-card-rates; run 2: sec-pay-high-interest-debt + fed-g19-card-rates; run 3: sec-pay-high-interest-debt + fed-g19-card-rates
column15: Pay down high-interest credit card balances first, before putting extra money into investments.
column16: Credit card interest is usually high, with the average rate on accounts that are charged interest at 21.52%. Investment returns are never certain, so paying off that debt is a guaranteed saving, while investing carries risk. Regulator guidance says no investment strategy consistently pays off as well as, or with less risk than, eliminating high interest debt.

column3: Keep an emergency fund that covers a few months of expenses.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Keep an emergency fund that covers a few months of living expenses.
column16: Basic consumer finance guidance widely recommends setting aside cash for a few months of expenses so a job loss, medical bill or car repair does not push you into debt. The exact amount depends on how stable your income is and how many people rely on it, but the core idea is sound.

column3: Renting is throwing money away.
column9: Absolute language; One size fits all
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: Paying rent is a waste of money compared with buying a home.
column16: Rent pays for housing, flexibility and often lower upfront and repair costs, so it is not simply lost money. Owning builds equity but also carries interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance and the cost of selling, and whether it beats renting depends on prices, rates, how long you stay and your local market. Basic consumer finance guidance treats it as a trade-off, not a rule.

column3: Make $5,000 a week from home with my course. Only 10 spots left.
column13: run 1: none; run 2: none; run 3: none
column15: A poster says you can earn $5,000 a week from home by buying their course, and that only 10 spots remain.
column16: The post exists to sell a course, and the income figure is the hook that drives the sale. A large, steady weekly income with no stated skills, hours or costs is not something basic consumer finance guidance supports. The limited spots add pressure to decide before you can check the details.
